decks.title: Resources and Development — Part 1: Resources, Planning and Land
goals: Classify resources by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status of development
Explain sustainable development, the Earth Summit and Agenda 21
Explain the need for and the stages of resource planning in India
Interpret land-use data and explain land degradation and its conservation
Practise classifying a resource and reading a land-use table step by step

slides.heading: Resources and Development
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what makes something a **resource**, how resources are **classified**, why India must **plan** their use, and how we use and misuse our **land**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a resource is, types of resources, development and sustainability, resource planning in India, and land use and land degradation
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Look around you. The water in your tap, the electricity in the fan, the wood of your desk, even the land under your school: all of these are resources. But are they free gifts of nature? And will they last forever? In this part we learn how geographers classify resources, why India needs to plan their use carefully, and what is happening to our most basic resource, land.

slides.heading: What turns nature into a resource?
slides.body_md: A **resource** is anything in our environment that can meet our needs, provided it is **technologically accessible**, **economically feasible** and **culturally acceptable**.

nodes.label: Nature: land, water, minerals, sunlight, plants and animals
Technology: tools and know-how to use it

visual.alt: Flow diagram: nature, technology and institutions together turn things in the environment into resources that meet human needs

slides.narration: Coal lay underground for millions of years before it became a resource. What changed? People learned how to mine and burn it, it became worth the cost, and society accepted its use. So resources are not simply free gifts of nature. Human beings, through technology and institutions, turn materials of nature into resources. Remember the three tests: can we reach it, can we afford it, and do we accept it?

slides.heading: Four ways to classify resources

nodes.label: Status of development: potential, developed, stock, reserves

visual.alt: Tree diagram: resources are classified on four bases: origin into biotic and abiotic; exhaustibility into renewable and non-renewable; ownership into individual, community, national and international; and status of development into potential, developed, stock and reserves

slides.narration: The same resource can be classified in four different ways, depending on the question you ask. Where does it come from? That is origin. Will it run out? That is exhaustibility. Who owns it? That is ownership. How far have we developed it? That is status of development. Learn the four bases and their categories as a tree; almost every question in this topic hangs from one of its branches.

slides.heading: Origin and exhaustibility
slides.body_md: Some non-renewable resources, such as **metals**, can be recycled; fossil fuels are **used up** once burnt.

rows: Can be renewed by physical, chemical or mechanical processes
Solar and wind energy, water, forests, wildlife
Form over millions of years; can be used up

visual.alt: Table: biotic resources have life, such as forests and fisheries; abiotic resources are non-living, such as rocks and metals; renewable resources can be renewed, such as solar energy and water; non-renewable resources take millions of years to form, such as coal and petroleum

slides.narration: Origin is the easiest test: is it living or not? Exhaustibility asks whether nature can replace it in our lifetime. Sunlight and wind keep coming. Coal and petroleum took millions of years to form, so once they are burnt, they are gone. A small but useful point: metals are non-renewable, but they can be recycled, while fossil fuels cannot. That makes a neat two-mark answer.

slides.heading: Who owns a resource?
slides.body_md: The government can even acquire private property for the public good, because land ultimately falls under the nation.

rows: A farmer's field, a house, an orchard, a private well
Village pond, grazing ground, burial ground, public park, playground
Minerals, water, forests, wildlife and land within the borders; territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles
Ocean resources beyond 200 nautical miles of the Exclusive Economic Zone

visual.alt: Table of ownership: individual resources are privately owned, such as a field or house; community resources are shared, such as a village pond; national resources include minerals and territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles; international resources lie beyond 200 nautical miles of the Exclusive Economic Zone

slides.narration: Ownership asks who can use it and who decides. Your family's field is individual. The village pond that everyone uses is community. Minerals and forests within India's borders belong to the nation, even under private land. And far out at sea, beyond two hundred nautical miles of a country's Exclusive Economic Zone, no single country can take the resources without the agreement of international institutions.

slides.heading: Quick check: who owns the pond?
slides.body_md: Classify the village pond by ownership.
slides.narration: Ask yourself: who is allowed to use this pond, one family or everyone in the village?

slides.heading: Status of development

rows: Found in a region but not yet used
Wind and solar energy of Rajasthan and Gujarat
Surveyed; quantity and quality worked out; in use
Could meet needs, but the technology to use it is lacking
Hydrogen in water as a fuel
Usable with today's technology, but saved for later

visual.alt: Table of status of development: potential resources exist but are unused, like Rajasthan's wind and sun; developed resources are surveyed and in use; stock needs technology we lack, like hydrogen in water; reserves can be used with existing technology but are kept for the future, like water in dams

slides.narration: This is the trickiest classification, so focus on one question: what is stopping us from using it? If nothing is stopping us but we simply have not started, it is potential. If we are already using it after surveys, it is developed. If the technology is missing, it is stock. And if we can use it but choose to save it for later, it is a reserve. Technology is the key difference between stock and the rest.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying one resource four ways
slides.body_md: Question: *Classify the wind blowing along an imagined coast in Gujarat, where no turbines have yet been built, on all four bases.*
bullets: Step 1 — Origin: wind is not living, so it is **abiotic**.
Step 2 — Exhaustibility: wind keeps blowing and is not used up, so it is **renewable**.
Step 3 — Ownership: it lies within India's borders, so it is a **national** resource.
Step 4 — Status: technology exists but nothing is built yet, so it is **potential**.
Step 5 — Check the trap: it is not stock, because we do have the technology.

visual.alt: Table: the wind is abiotic because it is non-living, renewable because it is not used up, national because it lies within the country, and potential because it is usable but not yet developed

slides.narration: When a question says classify, go base by base and always give a reason. Here the answer changes if the facts change. If turbines are built next year, the same wind becomes a developed resource. That is exactly what examiners like to test with case-based questions, so read the situation carefully before deciding the status of development.

slides.heading: When resource use goes wrong
slides.body_md: Using resources **indiscriminately** has led to three big problems:
bullets: Resources **used up** to feed the greed of a few.
A few people **control most resources**, widening the gap between rich and poor.
**Global ecological crises**: global warming, ozone layer depletion, environmental pollution and land degradation.
slides.narration: Resources made modern life possible, but careless use has a cost. Some resources are being used up to satisfy the greed of a few. Because some people control most of the resources, the gap between rich and poor grows. And the whole planet faces crises like global warming and pollution. The answer is not to stop development, but to change the way we develop. That idea is called sustainable development.

slides.heading: Towards sustainable development
slides.body_md: **Sustainable development** meets today's needs **without harming the environment** or the ability of **future generations** to meet theirs.

nodes.label: 1968: Club of Rome calls for systematic resource conservation
1987: Brundtland Commission report brings in the idea of sustainable development
June 1992: Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro
Agenda 21: every local government draws up its own plan

visual.alt: Timeline: in 1968 the Club of Rome called for systematic conservation; in 1987 the Brundtland Commission report introduced sustainable development; in June 1992 the Earth Summit met in Rio de Janeiro; and Agenda 21 asked every local government to draw up its own plan

slides.narration: Think of resources like a family's savings. Spending it all today leaves nothing for your children. Sustainable development means living on the interest, not the capital. In 1992 more than one hundred heads of state met at the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. They adopted Agenda 21, a plan for sustainable development in the twenty-first century, and asked every local government to prepare its own local version.

slides.heading: Quick check: Agenda 21
slides.body_md: What is one major objective of Agenda 21?
slides.narration: Remember: the twenty-one in Agenda 21 refers to a century, not a year.

slides.heading: India: rich here, poor there
slides.body_md: India's resources are **unevenly distributed**, so planning must be **balanced** at national, state, regional and local levels.

rows: Water, infrastructure and some vital minerals

visual.alt: Table: Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh are rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh in water but lacks infrastructure; Rajasthan in solar and wind energy but lacks water; Ladakh in cultural heritage but lacks water, infrastructure and some minerals

slides.narration: Look at the pattern in this table. Every region is rich in something and poor in something else. Jharkhand has coal and minerals but remains less developed. Arunachal Pradesh has water but few roads and power lines. Rajasthan has sun and wind but little water. This is why resource planning in India cannot be one plan for all. It must match each region's strengths and needs.

slides.heading: Three stages of resource planning
slides.body_md: India has worked on resource planning since the **First Five Year Plan**, launched after Independence.

nodes.label: 1. Identify and make an inventory of resources: survey, map, measure
2. Build a planning structure: technology, skills, institutions
3. Match resource plans with national development plans

visual.alt: Flow of the three stages of resource planning: first identify and make an inventory by surveying, mapping and measuring; second build a planning structure with technology, skills and institutions; third match resource plans with national development plans

slides.narration: Resource planning has three stages, and the order matters. First, find out what you have: survey, map and measure. You cannot plan what you have not counted. Second, set up the structure to use it: the right technology, trained people and institutions. Third, fit these plans into the country's overall development plans. Remember: availability alone is not development. Without technology and institutions, a resource-rich region can stay poor.

slides.heading: Conserving resources: need, not greed
slides.body_md: Irrational consumption and over-use of resources lead to social, economic and environmental problems. **Conservation** at every level is essential.
bullets: Gandhiji believed the earth has enough for everyone's needs but not for anyone's greed.
He blamed greedy, selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology.
He favoured production by the masses over mass production by machines.
slides.narration: Mahatma Gandhi gave a simple test for using resources: is this for my need, or for my greed? He believed nature can provide for everyone's needs but not for anyone's greed. He worried that big machines and mass production would exhaust resources and put them in a few hands. That is why he preferred production by the masses, in villages and small workshops. It is an old idea that sounds very modern.

slides.heading: India's land: plains, mountains, plateaus
slides.body_md: **Plains** support agriculture and industry; **mountains** keep rivers flowing all year and support tourism and ecology; **plateaus** hold minerals, fossil fuels and forests.

visual.alt: Bar chart of India's land by relief: plains about 43 per cent, mountains about 30 per cent, plateaus about 27 per cent
visual.caption: Bars from left: 1 plains (about 43%), 2 mountains (about 30%), 3 plateaus (about 27%).

slides.narration: Land is our most basic resource: it holds up our homes, roads, farms and forests. India's land is roughly forty-three per cent plains, thirty per cent mountains and twenty-seven per cent plateaus. Each has its own value. The plains feed us and host industry. The mountains feed our rivers. The plateaus are our storehouse of minerals and forests. So land use must fit the land.

slides.heading: How India's land is used
slides.body_md: **Gross cropped area** = net sown area + area sown more than once in an agricultural year.

rows: Barren and waste land; land put to non-agricultural uses (settlements, roads, railways, industry)
Permanent pastures and grazing land; land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves; culturable waste land (idle for more than 5 agricultural years)
Current fallow (idle for 1 agricultural year or less); other than current fallow (idle for the past 1–5 agricultural years)
Area actually sown with crops in a year

visual.alt: Table of land-use categories: forests; land not available for cultivation, including barren land and non-agricultural uses; other uncultivated land, including pastures, tree crops and culturable waste land idle for more than five years; fallow land, current fallow for one year or less and other fallow for one to five years; and net sown area

slides.narration: Land use is decided by physical factors like relief, climate and soil, and by human factors like population, technology and tradition. Learn the categories carefully, especially the three time limits: one year or less is current fallow, one to five years is other fallow, and more than five years is culturable waste land. Net sown area is over eighty per cent in Punjab and Haryana but under ten per cent in some north-eastern states.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a land-use table
slides.body_md: An imagined District X has a reporting area of **5,000 km²**: forests 900, net sown area 2,650, culturable waste 150, current fallow 200, other fallow 150 (km²). 1,100 km² is sown more than once.
bullets: Step 1 — Net sown area share: 2,650 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = **53%**.
Step 2 — Gross cropped area: 2,650 + 1,100 = **3,750 km²**.
Step 3 — Forest share: 900 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = **18%**, well below the 33% target of the National Forest Policy (1952).
Step 4 — Idle but cultivable land: culturable waste 150 + other fallow 150 + current fallow 200 = **500 km²**.
Step 5 — Conclusion: the district could afforest waste land and bring fallow land back under crops.

visual.alt: Table of working: net sown area share is 53 per cent; gross cropped area is 3,750 square kilometres; forest share is 18 per cent against a target of 33; idle cultivable land is 500 square kilometres

slides.narration: Data questions reward a calm, step-by-step method. Write the formula, put in the numbers, and give the unit. A percentage is part divided by whole, times one hundred. Gross cropped area adds the land sown more than once. Then always finish with a conclusion, because the last part of a case question usually asks what the numbers mean. Here: too little forest, and some idle land that could be used.

slides.heading: Quick check: fallow land
slides.body_md: Classify land left uncultivated for the past one to five agricultural years.
slides.narration: Use the three time limits: one year or less, one to five years, more than five years.

slides.heading: Land degradation: who and where

headers: Where it is a major cause
rows: Deforestation; deep scars and overburden left behind
Dust settles on land and slows the infiltration of water

visual.alt: Table of land degradation: mining in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha causes deforestation; overgrazing in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra strips vegetation; over-irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh causes waterlogging and salinity; mineral dust slows infiltration; industrial effluents pollute land and water

slides.narration: Land degradation is mostly caused by people. The examiner often asks you to link a cause with a region, so learn this table as pairs. Mining in the mineral states of the east. Overgrazing in the dry west and centre. Over-irrigation in the canal-watered north-west. And dust from grinding limestone for cement, which settles on fields and stops rainwater soaking in.

slides.heading: How too much water ruins farmland
slides.body_md: More water is not always better: **over-irrigation** is a leading cause of degraded land in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

nodes.label: Too much canal water on the fields
Water evaporates, leaving salts in the topsoil

visual.alt: Flow: too much canal water raises the water table and causes waterlogging; evaporation leaves salts in the topsoil; the soil becomes saline and alkaline; and crop yields fall

slides.narration: This one surprises students. How can water damage a farm? When fields get far more water than crops need, the water table rises and the land stays soggy. As the water evaporates in the hot sun, it leaves its dissolved salts behind. Year after year, the soil turns salty and alkaline, and crops struggle. This is why drip irrigation and careful water use matter even in well-watered states.

slides.heading: Conserving land
slides.body_md: Each measure targets a cause: match the remedy to the problem.
bullets: **Afforestation** and proper management of **grazing**.
Planting **shelter belts** of trees; growing **thorny bushes** to stabilise sand dunes.
Proper management of **waste land**; **control of mining** activities.
Treating **industrial effluents** and wastes before disposal.
slides.narration: For every cause of land degradation there is a matching remedy. Mining scars can be refilled and replanted. Overgrazing needs managed pastures. Sand dunes need shelter belts and thorny bushes. Factory waste must be treated before it is released. In an exam answer, pair each measure with the problem it solves. That simple habit turns a list into an explanation and earns the full marks.

slides.heading: Quick check: too much water
slides.body_md: Which state suffers land degradation mainly from over-irrigation?
slides.narration: Think of the north-western states with dense canal networks.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Accessible, feasible, acceptable; made by nature + technology + institutions
Origin, exhaustibility, ownership, status of development (potential, developed, stock, reserves)
Meet present needs without harming future ones; Rio 1992; Agenda 21
Inventory → planning structure → match with national plans
Plains 43%, mountains 30%, plateaus 27%; land-use categories; forest target 33%
Mining, overgrazing, over-irrigation, mineral dust, effluents; matching remedies

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1 covering resources, classification, sustainable development, resource planning, land and land degradation

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 in a minute. Things become resources through human effort. We classify them by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and development. Careless use led to the idea of sustainable development and Agenda 21. India must plan its unevenly spread resources in three stages. And our land, most of it plains, mountains and plateaus, is being degraded by mining, grazing and too much water, which we must reverse.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Stock vs reserves vs potential: ask "what stops us using it?" (technology → stock; choice → reserves; not started → potential).
Always give an **example** with each category of resource.
Fallow time limits: ≤ 1 year current fallow; 1–5 years other fallow; more than 5 years culturable waste land.
Link each cause of land degradation to its **region**, and each remedy to its cause.
Data items: formula, numbers, unit, then a one-line conclusion.
Agenda 21: Rio, 1992; the "21" is the 21st century.
slides.narration: Three habits will save marks in this part. Give an example with every category, because examiners award a mark for it. Learn the exact time limits for fallow land and the definition of stock versus reserves, because these are favourite traps. And in data questions, show your working and finish with what the numbers mean. Practise the classification tree until you can draw it from memory.

decks.title: Resources and Development — Part 2: Soils, Erosion and Conservation
goals: Explain how soil forms and why it is a precious renewable resource
Compare alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils
Identify the major soil types on a map of India
Explain the causes and types of soil erosion
Evaluate soil conservation methods and write a full-mark answer on them

slides.heading: Soil: the living skin of the land
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how **soil forms**, the **six major soil types** of India and where they are found, and how we can stop **soil erosion**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: how soil forms, the six soil types, the soil map of India, soil erosion and soil conservation
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Pick up a handful of soil. It may look like plain dirt, but it took nature a very long time to make it, and it feeds almost everything we eat. Soil is the most important renewable natural resource, yet it can be lost in a single season. In this part we meet India's six main soils, learn to find them on the map, and see how farmers protect them.

slides.heading: How soil forms
slides.body_md: Running water, wind, glaciers and decomposers all help in soil formation, along with chemical and organic changes.

nodes.label: Parent rock: weathering gives mineral particles
Climate: heat, cold, rain and wind break rocks
Relief: slope affects how soil collects
Vegetation and organisms: add humus; decomposers
Time: a few centimetres take a very long time

visual.alt: Flow diagram: parent rock, climate, relief, vegetation and organisms, and time together form soil

slides.narration: Five factors make a soil. Parent rock gives the raw material. Climate breaks the rock down. Relief decides whether soil collects or slides away. Plants, animals and decomposers add humus, the dark organic matter that makes soil fertile. And all of this needs time, a great deal of it. Even a few centimetres of soil can take an enormous span of time to form.

slides.heading: India's six major soils at a glance

rows: Deccan trap: Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh
Clayey; holds moisture; ideal for cotton
Eastern and southern Deccan; Odisha, Chhattisgarh
On crystalline igneous rocks; red from iron
Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, hilly Odisha and Assam
Texture varies with slope; acidic in snowy Himalayas

visual.alt: Table of six soils: alluvial in the northern plains, very fertile; black in the Deccan trap, clayey and good for cotton; red and yellow in the eastern and southern Deccan, red from iron; laterite in Kerala, Karnataka and other heavy-rain areas, leached and low in humus; arid in western Rajasthan, sandy and saline; forest soils in hilly areas

slides.narration: Here is your soil map in table form. Notice how each soil is tied to its region's rock and climate. Rivers made the alluvial plains. Lava made the black soils of the Deccan. Old crystalline rocks gave red soils. Heavy rain washed the laterites. The desert made arid soils. And the mountains have their own varied forest soils. If you know the reason, you can work out the region.

slides.heading: Alluvial soil
slides.body_md: The most widespread and important soil. Deposited by the **Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra** systems across the **northern plains**, it also reaches Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor and forms the **deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri**.
bullets: Made of sand, silt and clay in varying proportions; coarser near the foothills (duars, chos, terai).
Rich in **potash, phosphoric acid and lime**.
Ideal for **sugarcane, paddy, wheat**, other cereals and pulses.
Intensively cultivated and densely populated; soils in drier areas are more alkaline but productive with treatment and irrigation.

visual.alt: Table: alluvial soil is rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime and suits sugarcane, paddy, wheat, cereals and pulses

slides.narration: Alluvial soil is a gift of the rivers. Every flood lays down a fresh layer of fine sediment brought from the mountains. That is why the northern plains are so fertile, so intensively farmed and so densely populated. Notice also the coastal deltas in the east, where the rivers of the peninsula meet the sea.

slides.heading: Bangar and Khadar
columns:
**Bangar (old alluvium)**

- Found on higher ground, away from the river
- Higher concentration of **kankar nodules**
- Less fertile

**Khadar (new alluvium)**

- Found on the flood plains, renewed often
- **More fine particles**
- **More fertile**
slides.narration: Alluvial soils come in two ages. Bangar is the older alluvium on higher ground, which the floods no longer reach, and it is full of hard kankar nodules. Khadar is the newer alluvium on the flood plains, refreshed by floods, finer and more fertile. A memory trick: Khadar lies close to the river and gets fresh soil, while Bangar sits on the higher bank and keeps its old, kankar-filled soil.

slides.heading: Quick check: Khadar
slides.body_md: How does Khadar differ from Bangar?
slides.narration: Think: which one does the river renew with fresh, fine sediment?

slides.heading: Black soil (regur)
slides.body_md: Formed from the **lava rocks (basalt) of the Deccan trap**, where climate and parent rock together decide the soil.

rows: Plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh; along the Godavari and Krishna valleys
Holds moisture for a long time
Rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, lime; poor in phosphoric content
Deep cracks in hot weather (aeration); sticky when wet, so tilled after the first shower or before the monsoon

visual.alt: Table of black soil properties: found on the Deccan plateaus, extremely fine and clayey, holds moisture, rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime but poor in phosphoric content, cracks in summer and is sticky when wet, and is best for cotton

slides.narration: Black soil is the farmer's friend in a dry region because it holds water so well. In summer it cracks deeply, which lets air into the soil, almost like the soil breathing. But when it is soaked it becomes so sticky that ploughs and bullocks get stuck, so farmers plough right after the first shower. Remember the one weakness: it is poor in phosphorus.

slides.heading: Red and yellow soil and laterite soil
slides.body_md: The word **laterite** comes from the Latin *later*, meaning brick.

rows: On crystalline igneous rocks in areas of low rainfall
In tropical and subtropical climates with alternate wet and dry seasons; intense leaching by heavy rain
Eastern and southern Deccan; Odisha, Chhattisgarh; southern parts of the middle Ganga plain; piedmont zone of the Western Ghats
Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh; hilly areas of Odisha and Assam
Red from diffusion of iron; yellow when hydrated
Low humus (heat destroys decomposers); acidic; poor in nutrients
With manure and conservation: tea, coffee in the southern hills; cashew on red laterite

visual.alt: Table comparing red and yellow soil, formed on crystalline rocks in low rainfall areas and red from iron, with laterite soil, formed by intense leaching under heavy rain, low in humus and acidic, but used for tea, coffee and cashew after conservation and manuring

slides.narration: These two soils are often confused. Red soil is about rock and low rainfall: old crystalline rocks, with iron giving the red colour. Laterite is about heavy rain and heat: rain washes out the nutrients, a process called leaching, and heat kills the decomposers, so there is little humus. Yet with care, laterite hills in the south grow some of India's finest tea and coffee.

slides.heading: Arid soil and forest soil
bullets: **Arid soil**: red to brown, **sandy** and **saline**; in some areas common salt is obtained by evaporating its water.
Lacks **humus and moisture** because of the dry climate and fast evaporation; calcium increases downwards, forming a **kankar** layer that restricts water infiltration.
With **proper irrigation** it becomes cultivable, as in **western Rajasthan**.
**Forest soil**: found in hilly and mountainous areas with enough rain forests; **loamy and silty** on valley sides, **coarse-grained** on upper slopes.
In the **snow-covered Himalayas** it is acidic with **low humus**; on river terraces and alluvial fans lower down it is **fertile**.
slides.narration: Two contrasting soils. Arid soil belongs to the desert: sandy, salty, short of humus and water, with a hard kankar layer beneath that stops water sinking in. Give it water through irrigation and it can grow crops, as western Rajasthan shows. Forest soil belongs to the mountains and changes with the slope. High up in the snow it is thin and acidic, but down in the valleys it can be very fertile.

slides.heading: Quick check: why so little humus?
slides.body_md: Why is the humus content of laterite soil low?
slides.narration: Think about what high temperatures do to the tiny organisms that make humus.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: soils on the map of India
slides.body_md: Board map work asks you to **identify the major soil types** on an outline political map of India. Practise turning clues into regions.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the clue: "lava, cotton, cracks" → **black soil**; "river-deposited, northern plains" → **alluvial**.
Step 2 — Find a landmark: the **Deccan plateau** in Maharashtra for black soil; the **Ganga** from Punjab to West Bengal for alluvial soil.
Step 3 — "Leaching, tea, coffee, cashew" → **laterite**: the Western Ghats in Kerala and Karnataka. "Sandy, saline, kankar" → **arid**: western Rajasthan.
Step 4 — Shade lightly, write the soil name inside or beside the area, and add the letter asked for (A, B or C).
Step 5 — One mark per correctly placed and labelled feature; a wrong state is a lost mark, so learn the regions in the table.

rows: Crystalline rocks, low rain, red from iron
Eastern and southern Deccan, Odisha, Chhattisgarh
Leaching, low humus, tea and coffee
Western Ghats of Kerala and Karnataka; hilly Odisha and Assam

visual.alt: Table matching map clues to soils and where to shade them: black on the north-western Deccan; alluvial on the northern plains and deltas; red and yellow on the eastern and southern Deccan; laterite on the Western Ghats of Kerala and Karnataka; arid in western Rajasthan; forest soil in the Himalayas

slides.narration: Map questions on soils are really clue questions. Each soil has a fingerprint: lava and cotton for black, rivers for alluvial, iron and low rain for red, heavy rain and leaching for laterite, sand and salt for arid, slopes for forest soil. Turn the clue into a soil, the soil into a region, and shade neatly with a clear label. Practise on a blank outline map of India at least three times before the exam.

slides.heading: What is soil erosion?
slides.body_md: **Soil erosion** is the removal of the soil cover and its washing down. Formation and erosion usually balance each other; human activity upsets that balance.

nodes.label: Human causes: deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining

slides.narration: Nature is always both making and removing soil, and normally the two balance. Trouble begins when people remove the plants that hold soil in place, by cutting forests, overgrazing, building and mining. Then water, wind and glaciers carry the loose soil away much faster than new soil can form. Even ploughing in the wrong direction on a slope can speed up erosion, as we will see.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a 5-mark answer on soil conservation
slides.body_md: Question: *What is soil erosion? Describe its causes and any three methods of soil conservation.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Mark 1: define soil erosion in one line (removal of soil cover and its washing down).
Step 2 — Mark 2: causes in one line: deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining; water, wind, glaciers; ploughing up and down slopes.
Step 3 — Marks 3–5: three methods, each with **how it works** and **where it suits** (contour ploughing, terraces, shelter belts or strip cropping).
Step 4 — Use the key terms: contour lines, terraces, shelter belts, strip cropping, sand dunes.
Step 5 — Check the count: five distinct points, about 120 words; no mark for repeating one method in other words.

slides.narration: Look at how the question has three parts: define, causes, methods. Your answer should mirror that, so the examiner can tick each part. The commonest mistake is to name the methods without saying how they work. A name alone may earn half a mark; the name plus the mechanism earns the full mark. And keep it to about one hundred and twenty words.

notes.title: Resources and Development — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Resources and their types
sections.body_md:
A **resource** is anything in the environment that can satisfy human needs, as long as it is **technologically accessible**, **economically feasible** and **culturally acceptable**. Resources are **not free gifts of nature**: nature, technology and institutions interact, and human activity turns materials into resources.

**Four bases of classification**
- **Origin:** biotic (from the biosphere, with life: people, flora and fauna, fisheries, livestock) and abiotic (non-living: rocks, metals).
- **Exhaustibility:** renewable (renewed by physical, chemical or mechanical processes: solar and wind energy, water, forests, wildlife; some are continuous or flow resources like wind and water) and non-renewable (formed over a very long geological time: minerals, fossil fuels; metals can be recycled, fossil fuels cannot).
- **Ownership:** individual (fields, houses, orchards, wells), community (village ponds, grazing grounds, burial grounds, parks, playgrounds), national (all minerals, water, forests, wildlife and land within the borders and the territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles; the state can acquire private property for public good) and international (ocean resources beyond 200 nautical miles of the Exclusive Economic Zone, used only with the agreement of international institutions).
- **Status of development:** potential (found but not used: wind and solar energy in Rajasthan and Gujarat), developed (surveyed, quantity and quality determined, in use), stock (could meet needs but technology is lacking: hydrogen from water) and reserves (a subset of stock usable with existing know-how but kept for the future: water in dams, forests).

key_terms.definition_md: Anything in the environment that meets human needs and is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Materials that could meet human needs but which we lack the technology to use.
Part of the stock that can be used with present technology but is kept for future use.
A resource found in a region but not yet used.

visual.alt: Tree of the four bases of classifying resources and their categories

sections.heading: 2. Development of resources and sustainable development
sections.body_md:
**Problems of indiscriminate use:** depletion of resources for the greed of a few; accumulation of resources in a few hands, dividing society into rich and poor; global ecological crises such as global warming, ozone layer depletion, pollution and land degradation.

**Sustainable development:** development that does not damage the environment, meeting present needs without compromising the needs of future generations.

**Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro (June 1992):** more than 100 heads of state met at the first International Earth Summit on environmental protection and socio-economic development. They signed declarations on global climatic change and biological diversity, endorsed the global Forest Principles and adopted **Agenda 21**.

**Agenda 21:** a programme for global sustainable development in the 21st century, to fight environmental damage, poverty and disease through global cooperation on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities. A major objective: every **local government** should draw up its own local Agenda 21.

**Milestones in conservation thinking:** the Club of Rome (1968) called for systematic conservation; the Brundtland Commission report *Our Common Future* (1987) brought in the term sustainable development.

key_terms.definition_md: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
The 1992 Rio declaration for global sustainable development in the 21st century, with local Agenda 21 plans.

visual.alt: Timeline: Club of Rome in 1968, Brundtland report in 1987, Rio Earth Summit in 1992 and Agenda 21

sections.heading: 3. Resource planning and conservation in India
sections.body_md:
India's resources are **unevenly distributed**: Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh are rich in minerals and coal; Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water but lacks infrastructure; Rajasthan has solar and wind energy but lacks water; Ladakh has a rich cultural heritage but lacks water, infrastructure and some vital minerals. So planning is needed at national, state, regional and local levels.

**Stages of resource planning**
1. Identification and inventory of resources across regions: surveying, mapping, qualitative and quantitative estimation and measurement.
2. Evolving a planning structure with appropriate technology, skills and institutions.
3. Matching resource development plans with overall national development plans.

India has worked at resource planning since the **First Five Year Plan**. Resources alone do not bring development: technology and institutions are needed too.

**Conservation:** Gandhiji held that the earth has enough for everyone's needs but not for anyone's greed. He blamed greedy individuals and exploitative modern technology, and preferred production by the masses to mass production.

key_terms.definition_md: A strategy for the balanced, judicious use of resources, region by region.

visual.alt: Table of uneven resource distribution: mineral states short of development, Arunachal Pradesh short of infrastructure, Rajasthan short of water, Ladakh short of water and infrastructure

sections.heading: 4. Land resources and land use
sections.body_md:
India's land: **plains about 43%** (agriculture and industry), **mountains about 30%** (perennial rivers, tourism, ecology), **plateaus about 27%** (minerals, fossil fuels, forests).

**Land-use categories**
1. Forests.
2. Land not available for cultivation: barren and waste land; land put to non-agricultural uses (buildings, roads, railways, industry).
3. Other uncultivated land excluding fallow: permanent pastures and grazing land; land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves; culturable waste land (left uncultivated for more than 5 agricultural years).
4. Fallow lands: current fallow (1 agricultural year or less); other than current fallow (the past 1–5 agricultural years).
5. Net sown area.

**Gross cropped area** = net sown area + area sown more than once in an agricultural year.

Land use depends on physical factors (relief, climate, soil) and human factors (population density, technology, culture and traditions). Net sown area is over 80% in Punjab and Haryana but under 10% in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Forest area is well below the **33%** recommended by the **National Forest Policy (1952)**.

key_terms.definition_md: The area sown with crops in a year, counted once.
Net sown area plus the area sown more than once in the same agricultural year.
Cultivable land left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years.
Land left uncultivated for one agricultural year or less.

sections.heading: 5. Land degradation and conservation
sections.body_md:
**Causes (human):**
- **Mining** → deforestation: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha.
- **Overgrazing:** Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra.
- **Over-irrigation** → waterlogging → salinity and alkalinity: Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh.
- **Mineral processing** (grinding limestone for cement, calcite and soapstone for ceramics) → dust that slows the infiltration of water into the soil.
- **Industrial effluents** → water and land pollution.

**Conservation measures:** afforestation and proper management of grazing; planting shelter belts; control of overgrazing; stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes; proper management of waste lands; control of mining; proper discharge and disposal of industrial effluents and wastes after treatment.

key_terms.definition_md: A fall in the quality and productivity of land, mostly caused by human activities.
Saturation of soil by water when the water table rises, often from over-irrigation.

sections.heading: 6. Soil as a resource: formation and classification
sections.body_md:
Soil is a vital **renewable natural resource**: plants grow in it and countless organisms live in it. It takes a very long time to form even a few centimetres. **Factors:** relief, parent rock, climate, vegetation and other life forms, and time; weathering by temperature changes, running water, wind and glaciers, and the work of decomposers.

- **Alluvial:** most widespread; northern plains (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra), a corridor into Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Sand, silt and clay; coarser near the foothills (duars, chos, terai). **Bangar** = old alluvium with kankar nodules; **Khadar** = new, finer and more fertile. Rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime; sugarcane, paddy, wheat, cereals, pulses. Intensively cultivated and densely populated.
- **Black (regur):** Deccan trap (basalt lava): plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, and the Godavari and Krishna valleys. Extremely fine, clayey; holds moisture; rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime; poor in phosphoric content; deep cracks in hot weather (aeration); sticky when wet, so tilled after the first shower or in the pre-monsoon period. Ideal for **cotton**.
- **Red and yellow:** on crystalline igneous rocks in low-rainfall parts of the eastern and southern Deccan; Odisha, Chhattisgarh, southern middle Ganga plain, piedmont of the Western Ghats. Red from the diffusion of **iron**; yellow when hydrated.
- **Laterite** (Latin *later*, brick): tropical and subtropical climate with alternate wet and dry seasons; **intense leaching** by heavy rain; low humus because high temperature destroys decomposers; acidic, poor in nutrients. Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, hilly Odisha and Assam. With manure, fertilisers and conservation: tea and coffee in the southern hills; cashew on red laterite (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala).
- **Arid:** red to brown, sandy, saline (common salt obtained in places); lacks humus and moisture; **kankar** in lower horizons restricts infiltration; cultivable with irrigation, as in western Rajasthan.
- **Forest:** hilly and mountainous areas; loamy and silty on valley sides, coarse on upper slopes; acidic with low humus in the snow-covered Himalayas; fertile on river terraces and alluvial fans.

New alluvium, finer and more fertile.
Black soil of the Deccan trap, ideal for cotton.
Washing out of soil nutrients by heavy rain.

sections.heading: 7. Soil erosion and soil conservation
sections.body_md:
**Soil erosion:** the denudation of the soil cover and its washing down. Soil formation and erosion normally balance; human activities (deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining) and natural forces (wind, glaciers, water) upset the balance.
- **Gully erosion:** rainwater carves deep channels (gullies) in clayey soil until the land cannot be farmed (**bad land**); in the Chambal valley such land is known as **ravines**.
- **Sheet erosion:** a thin, wide film of water running down a slope strips off the topsoil.
- **Wind erosion:** strong winds lift and carry away loose, dry soil.
- **Defective farming:** furrows cut up and down a slope become channels that let water rush down.

**Conservation:**
- **Contour ploughing:** ploughing along contour lines slows water flowing down slopes.
- **Terrace farming:** steps cut into slopes restrict erosion; well developed in the western and central Himalayas.
- **Strip cropping:** bands of grass between bands of crops stop the wind sweeping across large fields.
- **Shelter belts:** rows of trees that shelter fields; they have helped stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.

key_terms.definition_md: The removal of the soil cover and its washing down.
Land made unfit for cultivation by gullies; ravines in the Chambal basin.
Rows of trees planted to break the wind and protect fields.
Growing strips of grass between strips of crops to break the force of the wind.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up **stock** (technology lacking) and **reserves** (technology available, kept for future).
- Fallow time limits: **current** ≤ 1 year; **other** 1–5 years; **culturable waste** > 5 years.
- Writing that black soil is rich in phosphorus: it is **poor** in phosphoric content.
- Explaining laterite's low humus without **heat destroying decomposers** and **leaching**.
- Naming a conservation method without saying **how it works**.
- Forgetting the **region** when asked about causes of land degradation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points (about 40 words); 3 marks: three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks: five distinct points (about 120 words); for comparisons, five heads with both soils on each.
- Data or case items: working + answer + unit, then a one-line interpretation.
- **Map work** (Geography carries 3 map marks in the board paper): one mark for each soil type correctly identified and labelled on the outline map of India.

**Sources in practice.** SOYL source items (field notebooks, letters, newspaper reports) and data tables are written by SOYL with imagined places and numbers; your board paper will use its own case.

cards.back_md: It meets human needs and is **technologically accessible**, **economically feasible** and **culturally acceptable**.

cards.front_md: Why are resources **not free gifts of nature**?
cards.back_md: Human activity, through **technology and institutions**, turns materials of nature into resources.
**Origin**, **exhaustibility**, **ownership**, **status of development**.
Biotic: have life (forests, fisheries, livestock). Abiotic: non-living (rocks, metals).
Renewable can be replenished (sun, wind, water, forests). Non-renewable take **millions of years** to form (coal, petroleum, minerals).
**Individual**, **community** (village pond), **national** (minerals, territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles), **international** (oceans beyond 200 nautical miles of the EEZ).
Found in a region but **not yet used**, e.g. wind and solar energy of Rajasthan and Gujarat.
**Stock**: we lack the technology (hydrogen in water). **Reserves**: usable with present technology but **kept for the future** (water in dams).
Development that meets present needs **without compromising the needs of future generations** and without damaging the environment.
**June 1992, Rio de Janeiro**; over 100 heads of state; adopted **Agenda 21**.
Global sustainable development; every **local government** to draw up its own **local Agenda 21**.
1. **Inventory** (survey, map, measure). 2. **Planning structure** (technology, skills, institutions). 3. **Match** with national development plans.

cards.front_md: Example: rich in one resource, short of another
cards.back_md: **Rajasthan**: solar and wind energy, but little water. **Arunachal Pradesh**: water, but little infrastructure.
Enough for everyone's **need**, not for anyone's **greed**; production by the masses, not mass production.
Plains **~43%**, mountains **~30%**, plateaus **~27%**.

cards.front_md: Fallow and waste land time limits
cards.back_md: Current fallow **≤ 1 year**; other fallow **1–5 years**; culturable waste land **> 5 years**.
**Net sown area + area sown more than once** in the same agricultural year.

cards.front_md: Forest target of the National Forest Policy (1952)
cards.back_md: **33%** of the geographical area.
Mining → **Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, MP, Odisha**; overgrazing → **Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra**; over-irrigation → **Punjab, Haryana, western UP**.
Waterlogging raises the water table; evaporation leaves salts, so soil turns **saline and alkaline**.
**Parent rock, climate, relief, vegetation and organisms, time.**
Bangar: **old** alluvium, more **kankar**. Khadar: **new**, finer, **more fertile**.

cards.front_md: Black soil: rich in / poor in
cards.back_md: Rich in **calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, lime**; poor in **phosphoric content**.

cards.front_md: Why is black soil good for cotton?
cards.back_md: Fine **clayey** texture that **holds moisture** for long; cracks aerate it.
Diffusion of **iron** in crystalline and metamorphic rocks (yellow when hydrated).
**Intense leaching** by heavy rain in wet-dry tropical climates; low humus because **heat destroys decomposers**.
Sandy, **saline**, lacks humus and moisture; **kankar** layer restricts infiltration; cultivable with **irrigation**.
Running water cuts deep **gullies**; land becomes **bad land**; called **ravines** in the **Chambal** basin.
Sheet: water flows as a sheet and strips topsoil. Wind: wind blows loose soil off flat or sloping land.
**Contour ploughing** (slows water), **terraces** (steep slopes), **strip cropping** (breaks wind), **shelter belts** (stabilise dunes).
Give the **name + how it works + where it suits** for each method.
Turn the clue into a soil, the soil into a region; shade, label, add the letter; one mark each.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **biotic** resource?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Biotic resources come from the biosphere and have life: people, plants, animals, fisheries, livestock.
Step 2: Fish are living organisms, so fisheries are biotic: (c).
Step 3: Iron ore, rock and sunlight are non-living (abiotic).

questions.stem_md: A resource whose amount and quality are known from surveys, and which is now being used, is called
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A developed resource has been surveyed, and its quantity and quality are known for use.
Step 2: So (b).
Step 3: Potential resources exist but are not yet used; stock needs technology we do not have; reserves can be used with present technology but are kept for the future.

questions.stem_md: A coastal district has strong, steady sea winds for most of the year, and the technology to use wind energy is available, but no wind turbines have been set up there yet. The wind energy of this district is best described as a
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The resource exists in the region and could be used (the technology exists), but it is not being used.
Step 2: That is a potential resource, so (a), like the wind and solar energy of Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Step 3: It is not developed (nothing has been built); it is not stock (stock is when the **technology** is lacking); "community" is about ownership, not development.

questions.stem_md: Water contains hydrogen, which could be a rich source of energy, but we do not yet have the advanced technology to use it on a large scale. Hydrogen in water is therefore an example of
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The material could meet human needs, but people lack the appropriate technology to use it.
Step 2: That is the definition of stock, so (d).
Step 3: Reserves and potential resources can be used with **existing** technology; developed resources are already in use.

questions.stem_md: A village pond is used by every family in the village for washing and for watering cattle. On the basis of ownership, the pond is
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Community-owned resources are open to all members of the community: grazing grounds, burial grounds, village ponds, public parks, playgrounds.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: Resources of the open ocean, beyond a country's 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone, are controlled by international institutions. On the basis of ownership, they are
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A country owns the resources within its boundaries and its territorial waters (up to 12 nautical miles), and has rights in its Exclusive Economic Zone.
Step 2: The open ocean beyond is regulated by international institutions, so these are international resources: (d).

questions.stem_md: In June 1992, leaders of more than a hundred countries gathered for the first International Earth Summit on the environment and development. Where was it held?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, the Earth Summit, met in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Step 2: So (a). It adopted Agenda 21.

questions.stem_md: One major objective of Agenda 21 is that

options.text_md: every country should stop using fossil fuels by the year 2021
only developed countries should conserve resources
every local government should draw up its own local Agenda 21 for sustainable development
all industries should be moved out of cities

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Agenda 21, adopted at Rio in 1992, aims at global sustainable development through cooperation on shared problems such as environmental damage, poverty and disease.
Step 2: A key objective is that every local government should prepare its own local Agenda 21, so (c).
Step 3: The "21" refers to the twenty-first century, not the year 2021 (a); the other options are invented.

questions.stem_md: Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water resources, yet it has developed only a small part of them. What does this show?

options.text_md: Having a resource is not enough for development: technology, infrastructure and institutions are also needed.
Water in Indian states belongs to international institutions.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The resource exists, but the infrastructure to use it is lacking.
Step 2: So availability is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for development; planning must bring in technology and institutions, (a).
Step 3: Water is renewable (b); (c) and (d) are false.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best sums up Mahatma Gandhi's view of resource conservation?

options.text_md: Big machines and mass production are the surest path to progress.
The earth can meet everyone's needs, but it cannot satisfy anyone's greed.
A country should sell its resources abroad to grow rich.
Nature cannot meet even the basic needs of people.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Gandhiji blamed greedy and selfish individuals and the exploitative nature of modern technology for the depletion of resources.
Step 2: He believed there is enough for everyone's needs but not for anyone's greed, so (b).
Step 3: He opposed mass production by machines and favoured production by the masses, so (a) is the opposite of his view.

questions.stem_md: About what share of India's land area is made up of plains?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: India's land is roughly 43% plains, 30% mountains and 27% plateaus.
Step 2: So (c). The plains support agriculture and industry.

questions.stem_md: Land that has been left uncultivated for the past one to five agricultural years is classified as
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Current fallow: left uncultivated for one agricultural year or less.
Step 2: Fallow other than current fallow: left uncultivated for the past one to five agricultural years, so (c).
Step 3: Culturable waste land: left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years. Barren land cannot be cultivated at all.

questions.stem_md: Culturable waste land is land that

options.text_md: is used for roads, railways and buildings
was left uncultivated in the current year only
has been left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Culturable waste land could be cultivated but has been left idle for more than five agricultural years, so (d).
Step 2: Forests and land under non-agricultural uses are separate categories; (c) describes current fallow.

questions.stem_md: According to the National Forest Policy of 1952, what share of India's geographical area should ideally be under forests?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The National Forest Policy (1952) set 33% of the geographical area as the desirable area under forests, to maintain ecological balance.
Step 2: So (b). India's actual forest area is well below this.

questions.stem_md: In which of these states is land degradation caused mainly by over-irrigation, which leads to waterlogging and an increase in salinity and alkalinity of the soil?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, over-irrigation is the main cause of land degradation.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: In Jharkhand and Odisha mining-led deforestation is the main cause; Mizoram has little irrigated land.

questions.stem_md: Near a cement factory, fine dust from the grinding of limestone settles on the surrounding fields. How does this degrade the land?

options.text_md: It adds organic matter to the soil.
It slows down the infiltration of water into the soil.
It causes waterlogging of the fields.
It increases the humus content of the soil.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Mineral processing such as grinding limestone (cement) or calcite and soapstone (ceramics) releases huge quantities of dust.
Step 2: The dust settles on the land and retards the infiltration of water into the soil, so (b).
Step 3: Dust adds no organic matter or humus, and it does not cause waterlogging.

questions.stem_md: A dry district of Gujarat is losing its grassland because herds graze the same land year after year. Which step would best check this land degradation?

options.text_md: Opening new mines in the grassland

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The cause is overgrazing, common in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
Step 2: The matching remedy is proper management of grazing land and control of overgrazing, so (d).
Step 3: The other options would add new causes of degradation (dust, waterlogging, mining).

questions.stem_md: Which is the most widely spread and important soil group of India?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Alluvial soil covers the entire northern plains (deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems) and the eastern coastal deltas.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: How does Khadar differ from Bangar?

options.text_md: Khadar is newer alluvium with more fine particles and is more fertile.
Khadar is older alluvium with many kankar nodules.
Khadar is found only on the Deccan plateau.
Khadar is formed from cooled lava.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Bangar is old alluvium with a higher concentration of kankar nodules.
Step 2: Khadar is new alluvium, with more fine particles, and is more fertile, so (a).
Step 3: Both are alluvial soils of river plains; lava-derived soil is black soil.

questions.stem_md: A farmer near Nagpur says: "My field is dark and clayey. It holds water well, cracks in May, and turns so sticky after heavy rain that I must plough soon after the first shower." Which soil is this?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dark colour, clayey texture, moisture retention, deep cracks in hot weather and stickiness when wet are features of black soil.
Step 2: Nagpur lies on the Deccan trap region of Maharashtra, where black soil is typical. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Black soil contains plenty of lime, potash, magnesium and calcium carbonate. Which nutrient is it usually short of?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Black soils are rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime.
Step 2: They are generally poor in phosphoric content, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Why is the humus content of laterite soil low?

options.text_md: Because it is formed from cooled lava
Because high temperatures destroy most decomposers such as bacteria, and heavy rain leaches the soil
Because it is deposited by rivers every year
Because the climate is too cold for plants to grow

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Laterite forms in tropical and subtropical climates with alternate wet and dry seasons, where heavy rain causes intense leaching.
Step 2: High temperatures destroy most micro-organisms, particularly decomposers like bacteria, so little humus forms, (b).
Step 3: (a) describes black soil, (c) alluvial soil, and (d) is the opposite of the climate.

questions.stem_md: Red soil looks red because of

options.text_md: the diffusion of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks
the salt content of the soil

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Red soils develop on crystalline igneous rocks in areas of low rainfall.
Step 2: Their reddish colour comes from the diffusion of iron, so (a). In hydrated form they look yellow.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about arid soils is correct?

options.text_md: They are rich in humus because of dense vegetation.
They are black and clayey and hold moisture well.
They are found mainly in the Ganga plains.
They are sandy and saline, lack humus and moisture, and a kankar layer below restricts the infiltration of water.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Arid soils range from red to brown, are generally sandy and saline, and lack humus and moisture because of the dry climate and high evaporation.
Step 2: Calcium content increases downwards, so the lower horizons have kankar, which restricts the infiltration of water. So (d).
Step 3: (a) is false, (b) describes black soil, (c) describes alluvial soil.

questions.stem_md: Running water cuts deep gullies into clayey soil until the land becomes unfit for cultivation. Such land is called
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Gully erosion makes land unfit for cultivation; this is called bad land.
Step 2: So (c). In the Chambal basin such land is called ravines.

questions.stem_md: A farmer on a hill slope ploughs his furrows straight up and down the slope. After a heavy storm, much of his topsoil has washed away. Why?

options.text_md: The furrows formed channels that let rainwater rush down the slope, carrying soil with it.
Ploughing up and down adds too much humus.
The furrows trapped too much water and caused waterlogging.
Wind blew the soil away because the field was flat.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Furrows running up and down a slope act as channels for the quick flow of water.
Step 2: Fast-flowing water carries away the topsoil, so (a). This is a defective farming method.
Step 3: The remedy is to plough along the contours, which slows the water.

questions.stem_md: A village on steep hill slopes in Uttarakhand wants to grow crops without losing its soil. Which method suits it best?

options.text_md: Planting shelter belts against desert winds
Ploughing up and down the slope

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: On steep slopes, steps (terraces) cut into the hillside create flat surfaces and slow the run-off, restricting erosion.
Step 2: Terrace farming is well developed in the western and central Himalayas, so (d).
Step 3: Strip cropping and shelter belts mainly check wind; ploughing up and down the slope increases erosion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Resources are not free gifts of nature.

**Reason (R):** Things in nature become resources only through human activity, using technology and institutions to make them useful.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: nature offers materials, but they become resources only when people can use them.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: humans transform things in nature into resources through technology and institutions. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Black soil is well suited to growing cotton.

**Reason (R):** Black soil develops deep cracks during hot weather.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: black soil is also called black cotton soil.
Step 2: R is true: deep cracks form in summer, which helps the soil get aerated.
Step 3: But the main reason it suits cotton is its fine clayey texture and great capacity to **hold moisture**, along with its nutrients. The cracks do not explain why cotton grows well, so (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Net sown area is over 80 per cent of the total area in Punjab and Haryana.

**Reason (R):** Most of Punjab and Haryana is mountainous and covered with forests.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: these states have very high net sown area.
Step 2: R is false: both are mainly fertile alluvial plains with little forest. So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ploughing along contour lines increases soil erosion on slopes.

**Reason (R):** Ploughing along contour lines slows down the flow of water down the slope.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: contour ploughing **reduces** erosion.
Step 2: R is true: furrows across the slope slow the run-off. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the hilly areas of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, laterite soils have become useful for growing tea and coffee.

**Reason (R):** Laterite soil is naturally low in humus, but soil conservation and adequate manuring make it productive.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: with conservation techniques, laterite soils in these hills grow tea and coffee.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: the soil is poor by nature, and conservation plus manures and fertilisers is what made it useful. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Rajasthan has a large potential for solar and wind energy.

**Reason (R):** Rajasthan is deficient in water resources.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: Rajasthan is well endowed with sunshine and wind.
Step 2: R is true: water is scarce there.
Step 3: Lack of water does not explain the solar and wind potential (that comes from clear skies, strong sunshine and open land). Both facts together show why resource planning must be region-specific. So (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Water held in a dam for future use is an example of reserves, because we already have the technology to use it.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Reserves are a subset of stock; the know-how exists and they are kept for future use, like the water stored in dams.
Step 2: So the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Arid soils are generally rich in humus.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The dry climate and high temperature make evaporation fast, so arid soils lack humus and moisture.
Step 2: So the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Land that has been left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years is called current fallow.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Current fallow is land left uncultivated for one agricultural year or less.
Step 2: Land left idle for more than five years is culturable waste land. So the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Terrace farming is well developed in the western and central Himalayas.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Steps cut into the slopes of the western and central Himalayas create terraces for farming.
Step 2: So the statement is true.

questions.stem_md: Resources such as coal and petroleum, which take millions of years to form, are called ___ resources.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Fossil fuels form over a very long geological time and cannot be replaced within a human lifetime.
Step 2: The answer is non-renewable.

questions.stem_md: Black soil is also known as ___ soil.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Black soil is called regur, and also black cotton soil because it suits cotton.
Step 2: The answer is regur.

questions.stem_md: Rows of trees planted to protect fields from strong winds are called ___.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Lines of trees that break the force of the wind are shelter belts; in western India they have helped stabilise sand dunes.
Step 2: The answer is shelter belts.

questions.stem_md: Match each soil with a region where it is typically found.

match_right.text_md: Hilly areas of Kerala and Karnataka

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Alluvial soil covers the northern plains (p–3).
Step 2: Black soil covers the Deccan trap plateaus of Maharashtra, Malwa and Saurashtra (q–4).
Step 3: Laterite soil occurs in Kerala, Karnataka and other areas of heavy rainfall (r–2).
Step 4: Arid soil covers western Rajasthan (s–1).

questions.stem_md: Match each soil conservation method with the problem it is best suited to.

match_right.text_md: Wind breaking up the soil of large open fields
Shifting sand dunes at the edge of a desert

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Contour ploughing slows water running down slopes (p–2).
Step 2: Terraces make steep slopes farmable (q–4).
Step 3: Strips of grass between crops break the force of the wind across large fields (r–1).
Step 4: Shelter belts stabilise sand dunes, as in western India (s–3).

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages of resource planning in India in the correct order.

options.text_md: Match the resource development plans with the overall national development plans
Identify and make an inventory of resources by surveying, mapping and measuring them
Set up a planning structure with the right technology, skills and institutions

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: First, find out what resources exist, where, and how much (inventory).
Step 2: Then build the structure (technology, skills, institutions) to develop them.
Step 3: Finally, fit these plans into the national development plans.
Step 4: So the order is b, c, a.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which over-irrigation degrades farmland, from cause to final effect.

options.text_md: As the water evaporates, salts are left behind in the topsoil
The soil turns saline and alkaline and crop yields fall
Fields receive far more canal water than the crops need
The water table rises and the land becomes waterlogged

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Excess irrigation water (c) raises the water table (d).
Step 2: Evaporation leaves salts in the topsoil (a).
Step 3: Salinity and alkalinity reduce yields (b).
Step 4: So the order is c, d, a, b.

marking_scheme.step: Correct order c, d, a, b

questions.stem_md:
On an outline political map of India, shade and label the area of:

**A.** the soil that is typical of the Deccan trap region and is ideal for cotton.

places.name: Black soil (Deccan trap: Maharashtra, Malwa, Saurashtra, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh)

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The clue (Deccan trap, cotton) points to black soil.
Step 2: Shade the north-western Deccan plateau: Maharashtra, Saurashtra (Gujarat), Malwa (Madhya Pradesh), and along the Godavari and Krishna valleys; label it "Black soil".

marking_scheme.step: A: Black soil (Deccan trap: Maharashtra, Malwa, Saurashtra, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh) correctly located and labelled

questions.stem_md:
On an outline political map of India, shade and label the area of:

**A.** the soil deposited by the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra river systems.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: River-deposited soil of the north is alluvial soil.
Step 2: Shade the northern plains from Punjab to Assam (and the eastern coastal deltas if asked); label it "Alluvial soil".

marking_scheme.step: A: Alluvial soil (northern plains) correctly located and labelled

questions.stem_md:
On an outline political map of India, shade and label the area of:

**A.** the soil that forms by intense leaching under heavy rain, and that grows tea, coffee and cashew after conservation.

places.name: Laterite soil (Western Ghats in Kerala and Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, hilly Odisha and Assam)
